title: LongHorizonUI: Robust Long-Horizon GUI Task Automation
one_liner: Add state snapshots, decision validation, and rollback recovery to keep GUI agents on track through 15+ step tasks.
lead: A GUI agent reads a screen, decides what to click, and executes the action. For short 3-step tasks (open app, click button, read result), that works. But real tasks need 20+ steps—navigate menus, fill forms, handle popups, adjust settings. Current agents forget where they are, make wrong turns, and crash into dead ends. LongHorizonUI adds three guardrails: clearer state snapshots so the agent knows what it sees, multi-level feedback checks before each action, and a rollback plan if a step goes wrong.

problem.h2: Short tasks work; long chains break
paras: A GUI agent is a program that looks at a screen image, uses an image-understanding model to read text and find buttons, decides what to click next, and moves the mouse. For a 3-step task—open the settings, click a checkbox, close the menu—this works fine. The model sees each screen clearly and the chain is so short that even a small mistake (misread a label) does not cascade.

Real tasks are not 3 steps. Opening a bank account needs 20 steps: navigate the website, enter personal details across 3 forms, upload a document, wait for a page to load, choose account type, confirm the choice, and finish. Each step depends on the last. If the agent misidentifies a button in step 7, step 8 lands on the wrong screen, and by step 12 the agent is hopelessly lost, clicking buttons that do not exist or filling fields it should have skipped. The longer the task, the worse the drift. At step 15 and beyond, most agents fail because they have no way to detect that they went wrong—they just keep clicking, making things worse.

Why does this happen? The agent's decision model (a large language model that reads screenshots) does not maintain a reliable memory of the full screen state. It sees one screenshot at a time. If the screen changes in an unexpected way, the agent keeps going with old assumptions. It has no way to step back and retry when something feels off. And it has no way to check: 'Did that click actually do what I expected?'

callout.html: GUI agents stay on track for 3–5 steps but lose their way in 15+ step tasks because they do not reliably track state, validate each decision, or recover from mistakes.

steps.text: Run a text recognizer and object detector on the screenshot; label each clickable element (button, text field, link) with a unique index so the agent always knows exactly what is on screen.
The decision model reads the labeled screenshot and the task goal, then outputs: click button 5, or type in field 3, etc.
The agent simulator (or real browser) carries out the click or keystroke.
Immediately take a new screenshot. Check: Did the screen change? Did the result match what the action should cause (new menu appeared, field filled, page loaded)? Or did something go wrong?
If validation fails, the agent rewinds to the last known good state and retries with a different action, rather than drifting further into a dead end.

object.h2: The three things the method changes
paras: LongHorizonUI modifies three parts of a typical GUI agent pipeline.

First, it upgrades state representation: instead of the agent seeing a raw screenshot, it sees a screen with every interactive element labeled with a number. This is done by running object detection and text recognition on every screenshot, which takes a few extra milliseconds but gives the decision model a much clearer view of what it can interact with.

Second, it adds a validation layer: after each action, the agent does not just assume success—it compares the new screenshot to what it expected, using a structured set of checks at different levels (Did the screen change at all? Did the right element highlight or open? Did the page load?).

Third, it wraps the action executor in a recovery system: if validation fails, the agent does not push forward; instead, it stores a 'checkpoint' of the last good screen and rewinds to it, allowing a retry.
object.object: State clarity, decision validation, and action rollback

hidden.h2: Action reliability: measuring mistakes across long chains
hidden.name: Action reliability across steps
paras: The core hidden quantity LongHorizonUI measures is: for a task with N steps, how many steps execute without any mistake? We call this 'action reliability across steps.' It is not a single number like accuracy (one task, pass or fail), but a trend: the fraction of steps that succeed, step by step, over a long chain.

Concretely: if a task has 20 steps and the agent completes steps 1–6 correctly, then step 7 fails (clicks the wrong button), and the agent rewinds and retries—the raw reliability at step 7 is low, but after rollback the agent succeeds at the retry. The paper measures both: the initial success rate (how often the first attempt works) and the corrected success rate after validation and rollback (how often the agent eventually gets past each step, even after retries).

This quantity is invisible in short tasks (a 3-step task always appears to work or fail as a whole), but it is the critical diagnostic in long tasks: where does the drift happen? Step 7? Step 12? Which steps stay reliable step-after-step, and which tend to fail? LongHorizonUI measures this because knowing which specific steps are error-prone lets the team add stronger validation or fallback actions at those points in the future.

heat.caption: Darker means step executed correctly. Step 7 failed initially (light) but recovered after rollback.

reads.html: For each step in a long task, did the agent click the right button? After validation and rollback, how many steps end up correct?

The paper calls this 'success rate' or 'pass rate per step' across the long-horizon benchmark (LongGUIBench). It splits the metric into 'initial accuracy' and 'post-recovery accuracy' because the difference between the two directly quantifies the value of rollback—if post-recovery accuracy is much higher, rollback is worth the cost.

mechanism.h2: Why clearer state, checked decisions, and rollback keep agents on track
paras: The root cause of failure in long tasks is information decay: each step, the agent's understanding of the current screen gets fuzzier. It started with a clear screenshot of a bank login page, but after 7 steps and 7 different pages, the decision model is working from outdated assumptions. It tries to click a button it saw two pages ago, or it assumes a field is empty when it is actually filled. The agent has no feedback loop, so it does not know it is lost until it is too late.

LongHorizonUI fixes this by adding three reinforcing mechanisms. First, it forces a clear state snapshot at every step: the agent does not see a blurry photo; it sees every clickable element labeled with a number. This reduces ambiguity—when the agent says 'click button 17,' there is no guessing which button it meant. Second, after each action, the agent checks the result against a structured set of expectations. Did the screen change? Did the expected new element appear, or did nothing happen? This feedback reaches the decision model before the next step, so drift is caught immediately. Third, when feedback catches a mistake, the agent rewinds to the last known good screen and retries with a different action, rather than compounding the error. This turns what would be a fatal wrong turn into a local recovery—the task backtrack from step 7 to step 6, fixes the mistake, and continues forward.

Why this works: long-horizon success is not about a single super-intelligent decision at each step; it is about catching and correcting small mistakes as they happen, before they cascade. By keeping state clear, checking results, and enabling retries, the agent can afford to make and recover from step-level mistakes. The overall success rate improves because the agent no longer drifts into dead ends.

stages.s: Detect objects and text; label each element with a number
Agent model reads labeled state and outputs next action
If check fails, rewind to last good state and retry
Proceed to next step only if validated

math.h2: Measuring progress: success rate before and after rollback
math.words: For a task with N steps, the unadjusted success rate is the number of steps that got the right result on the first try, divided by N. The corrected success rate includes retries after rollback.
symbols: number of steps where the initial action was correct
number of steps where the action was correct after rolling back and retrying
total number of steps in the task

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Task: 10 steps to open a bank account.
First attempt: steps 1–6 correct, step 7 wrong click, steps 8–10 also wrong (drift from the step 7 mistake).

After LongHorizonUI validation: Step 7 caught by feedback check. Agent rewinds to step 6, retries step 7 with a different button (now correct). Steps 8–10 now also correct because they are not built on the step 7 mistake.
The rollback strategy turned a 60% fail into a 100% pass by catching and fixing the single wrong step.

math.note: The difference between before and after rollback shows the value of validation: when a mistake is caught early, retrying at that step repairs the entire downstream chain.

items.b: Labeled state is ambiguous or wrong.
items.html: If the object detector or text recognizer misses an element or labels two buttons the same, the agent still makes the wrong choice. Labeling is a bottleneck: better detection leads to clearer state because the agent can read each label confidently, which leads to fewer mistakes because the agent is not guessing which button is which. This is not the paper's main focus, but it is a real constraint.

items.b: Validation checks are too strict or too loose.
items.html: If the feedback rules require perfect pixel-by-pixel match, legitimate screen variations (animation, loading spinner, font rendering) will cause false rollbacks. If the checks are too loose, real failures go undetected. The paper's 'multi-level' feedback (does the screen change? does the right element appear?) aims for a middle ground, but tuning this per application is an engineering challenge.

items.b: Rollback gets stuck in a loop.
items.html: If every action leads to a mistake and every retry also fails, the agent rewinds again and again and never moves forward, because each retry is based on the same decision model and the same screen, so nothing has changed. The paper includes a 'progress monitoring' system that detects infinite loops and gives up gracefully, but determining when to quit is a heuristic.

The paper shows the method works on a custom benchmark (LongGUIBench with tasks over 15 steps) and retains performance on standard benchmarks. The code is open-source, so it can be tested on new applications.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple GUI task: a web form with 10+ steps (e.g., an e-commerce checkout: select item, enter name, pick shipping, enter address across 3 fields, choose payment, confirm). Start with a baseline agent (no validation, no rollback), then turn on the three components one by one: first add state labeling, then add validation checks, then add rollback. Measure the success rate at each stage and show that both initial success (first try) and recovery success (after rollback) improve, because clearer state eliminates ambiguity in which button to click, validation catches mistakes before they compound, and rollback gives the agent a second chance to fix step-level errors.
demo.closing: The demo must show that an agent alone reaches step 6 and then gets lost, but with all three guardrails it completes all 10 steps. This proves that keeping state clear, validating decisions, and rolling back mistakes are what enable long-horizon success, because the three guardrails together prevent the cascade of small errors into total failure.
